{"id": "090427ea-96a5-446a-93f0-395d16b412ab", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "Switching to Elastic throughput is an online change. It causes no application downtime.

I checked us-east-1 in this agent space's account (012345678901_1) and found no EFS file systems there. If your file system is in another account or Region, tell me which one and I can look at it.

**Ways to switch**
- **Console:** Open the file system in the EFS console and choose **Edit**. Under **Throughput mode**, select **Elastic** and save.
- **CLI:**
  ```
  aws efs update-file-system \
    --file-system-id fs-xxxxxxxx \
    --throughput-mode elastic
  ```
- **API/SDK:** Call `UpdateFileSystem` with `ThroughputMode=elastic`. You don't need to pass a provisioned amount.

**Things to know**
- **Provisioned throughput:** If the file system is on Provisioned mode and you raised the amount or switched to it within the last 24 hours, you can't switch to Elastic until that window passes. Bursting mode has no such restriction.
- **Scaling and cost:** Elastic scales throughput up and down automatically, and you pay for the data you read and write. Set a CloudWatch alarm on `MeteredIOBytes` so a runaway workload doesn't surprise you on the bill.
- **Performance mode:** Elastic throughput needs the General Purpose performance mode. It isn't available on Max I/O file systems.
- **If throughput stays low afterward:** Elastic removes the throughput ceiling. Per-operation latency, client-side limits (instance network bandwidth, mount options such as NFS `rsize`/`wsize`, and single-threaded I/O) can still cap what you see.

If you share the file system ID, account and Region, I can check its current mode and metrics. I can also run the switch for you, and you'd approve it before it runs.", "type": "text"}], "created_at": null}
